newsitem.title: UK: British royal prone to blunders.
newsitem.headline: British royal prone to blunders.

text.p: Prince Philip's gaffe over guns on Thursday is just the latest blunder the loose-lipped consort has wrought upon Britain's protocol-crazy royal family.

Be it the shape of a Chinaman's eyes, the ingratitude of the unemployed or the Scots' fabled taste for whisky, Greek-born Philip has put his foot in it time and again since he married into the world's most watched royal family.

Yet again on Thursday, the palace was forced to say sorry on behalf of the 75-year-old prince -- a polar opposite to his tight-lipped wife Queen Elizabeth -- after he declared that members of shooting clubs were no more dangerous than golfers or cricketers.
"Prince Philip had no intention whatsoever of causing offence or distress to anyone and he is sorry if he has done so," said a Buckingham Palace spokesman.

His comments touched a raw nerve, coming months after lone gunman Thomas Hamilton shot dead 16 children and their teacher at a Scottish school. While voicing sympathy for the relatives, Philip said the public's reaction had not been rational.

"If a cricketer, for instance, suddenly decided to go into a school and batter a lot of people to death with a cricket bat, which he could do very easily, I mean are you going to ban cricket bats?" Philip, a keen hunter and shooter, said in a BBC radio interview due to be aired on Thursday evening.
It was vintage Philip: outspoken, unguarded and decidedly outside any definition of "politically correct".
For while some of the young royals are known for bearing their souls, sex lives and shopping habits, "Phil the Greek" is an anomaly among the older generation.

"I despair of the Duke of Edinburgh. This man is insensitive, selfish and ham-fisted," said Labour member of parliament Tony Banks. "A prolonged period of silence on his part would be much appreciated."
But prolonged silence is not the preferred option of the man whom the tabloid Daily Mirror on Thursday dubbed "Prince Foolip".
At the height of the British recession in 1981 he said: "Everybody was saying we must have more leisure. Now they are complaining they are unemployed."
-- During a visit to China in 1986 he described Peking as "ghastly" and told British students: "If you stay here much longer you'll all be slitty-eyed."
-- In 1995 the one-time sailor asked a Scottish driving instructor: "How do you keep the natives off the booze (drink) long enough to pass the test?"
-- In 1993, Philip told a Briton he met in Hungary: "You can't have been here that long -- you haven't got a pot belly."
-- He once said of Canada: "We don't come here for our health. We can think of other ways of enjoying ourselves."
-- The prince struck closer to home in 1966, declaring what many foreigners had long suspected: "British women can't cook."
-- Nor have stars escaped. In 1969, Philip asked heart-throb Tom Jones: "What do you gargle with, pebbles?". He compared Adam Faith's singing to bath water going down a plug hole.
